title: Mediator Pattern
oneLiner: Centralizes communication between objects so they talk to one hub instead of wiring directly to each other.

hero.name: Switchboard
hero.catchphrase: Don't talk to each other. Talk to me — I'll route it.
hero.power: Routes all communication between a group of objects through one central hub, removing their direct references to each other.
hero.weakness: All that routing logic has to live somewhere — Switchboard itself can bloat into a god-object if it absorbs too much responsibility.
hero.origin: Switchboard was summoned from a flight-booking UI where the date picker, seat selector, price display, and payment button all held direct references to each other — 12 wires between 4 widgets.

story.problem: A booking form's DatePicker calls SeatSelector directly, which calls PriceDisplay directly, which calls PaymentButton directly. Four widgets, twelve tangled direct references between them.
story.solution: Switchboard becomes the single hub. Every widget only talks to the Mediator — 'date changed', 'seat changed' — and the Mediator decides what happens next.
story.result: Widgets no longer know about each other at all. Adding a fifth widget means teaching the Mediator about it, not rewiring four existing ones.

before: Every widget holds direct references to several others
N widgets need up to N² wires between them
One widget's change can ripple unpredictably through the rest
after: Every widget only knows about the mediator
N widgets need only N connections, all to the hub
Changes are routed predictably through one central place

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A diagram shows twelve crossing wires directly connecting four form widgets to each other.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: I changed the date picker and the payment button broke. They're not even related! But somehow they're wired together.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: Switchboard appears at the center, and every wire redirects to plug into it instead.
panels.speaker: Switchboard
panels.dialogue: Stop wiring widgets directly to each other. Wire every one of them to ME. I'll route what needs to happen next.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: Each widget calls mediator.notify('dateChanged') instead of calling other widgets by name.
panels.speaker: Switchboard
panels.dialogue: You don't need to know who reacts to your change. Just tell me what happened — I know who needs to hear it.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: Twelve tangled wires collapse into four clean spokes, all connecting to Switchboard.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Changing the date picker only touches the mediator's routing logic now. The payment button is safe.

useWhen: A group of objects communicate in a tangled, many-to-many way that's hard to trace or change safely.
You want to add or remove participants without rewiring every existing one.
The coordination logic between components deserves to live in one place instead of scattered across all of them.
avoidWhen: Only two objects are involved — a direct reference is simpler than routing through a hub.
The 'communication' is really just a simple, one-directional data flow that doesn't need central coordination.
The mediator would just become a dumping ground for unrelated logic instead of focused coordination.
commonMistakes: Letting the mediator absorb business logic that belongs in the components themselves, turning it into a god-object.
Building a Mediator for a simple two-object relationship that never needed centralizing.
Not documenting which events the mediator handles, making its routing logic a black box to new contributors.
Confusing Mediator (centralizes communication between peers) with Observer (one subject broadcasts to many independent subscribers).
explanation.realWorldExample: Air traffic control coordinating planes that never talk to each other directly, chat room servers routing messages between clients, and UI form-orchestration logic (like a wizard coordinating multiple steps) are all Mediator.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: This sounds like Observer — a central point some objects talk through.

conversation.speaker: Switchboard
conversation.message: Related, but Observer is one-directional: a Subject broadcasts, Observers just listen. I coordinate a genuine back-and-forth conversation between multiple peers who'd otherwise be tangled together.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How do I stop you from becoming a god-object?

conversation.speaker: Switchboard
conversation.message: Keep my job strictly to ROUTING — deciding who hears what. The actual business logic should stay inside each widget, not migrate into me.

codeBattle.scenario: Your flight-booking form has a date picker, seat map, price display, and payment button — and changing any one of them currently requires updating direct references in two or three others.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: Switchboard replaces the tangled many-to-many wiring between widgets with a single hub each widget talks to, so adding or changing a widget no longer ripples through the others.

quiz.question: What problem does Mediator solve?
options: A group of objects reference each other directly in a tangled, hard-to-change way
An object needs to guarantee exactly one instance
A complex object needs to be assembled step by step
An algorithm needs to be swapped at runtime
quiz.answer: A group of objects reference each other directly in a tangled, hard-to-change way
quiz.explanation: Mediator exists to replace many-to-many direct coupling with one-to-many coupling through a hub.

quiz.question: After introducing a Mediator, how do the participating objects communicate?
options: They notify the mediator, which decides how to route the event to others
They still call each other directly, just with an extra logging step
They communicate through a shared global variable
They no longer communicate at all
quiz.answer: They notify the mediator, which decides how to route the event to others
quiz.explanation: The mediator becomes the single point that knows how each event should propagate.

quiz.question: What's the main risk of the Mediator pattern?
options: The mediator can absorb too much logic and become a god-object
It always makes communication slower than direct references
It requires every participant to be a Singleton
It prevents adding new participants entirely
quiz.answer: The mediator can absorb too much logic and become a god-object
quiz.explanation: Centralizing coordination is powerful, but the mediator can become bloated if it absorbs logic that belongs elsewhere.

quiz.question: How does Mediator differ from Observer?
options: Mediator coordinates two-way communication among peers; Observer is one subject broadcasting to independent listeners
They are identical patterns with different names
Observer requires a central hub; Mediator does not
Mediator can only have one participant
quiz.answer: Mediator coordinates two-way communication among peers; Observer is one subject broadcasting to independent listeners
quiz.explanation: The direction and symmetry of communication is the key difference between the two patterns.
